analysis.one_liner: Requires foreign financial institutions to report US account holders to crack down on offshore tax evasion.
analysis.headline: The offshore tax-reporting bill never got a committee vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 3933, the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act of 2009, was a tax-enforcement bill aimed at Americans who hold money abroad without reporting it. It would require foreign financial institutions — and some foreign companies — to report their US account holders to the IRS, and would deny a tax deduction for interest on non-registered bonds issued outside the United States [S2]. Rep. Charles Rangel, then chair of the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, introduced it on October 27, 2009; it was referred to his own committee the same day [S5]. No markup was scheduled, no vote was taken in committee or on the House floor, and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary, honest US taxpayers, whose taxes are higher when wealth is hidden offshore, and the IRS, which would gain a new tool to detect unreported foreign income. The bill shifts the burden of identifying US account holders onto foreign financial institutions themselves rather than relying on individual taxpayers to self-report [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires foreign financial institutions to report income from assets held abroad by US persons, closing a gap where offshore accounts went undetected [S2].
Extends reporting duties to foreign nonfinancial entities as well, not just banks [S2].
Denies a tax deduction for interest on non-registered bonds issued outside the United States, discouraging a channel for unreported foreign income [S2].

analysis.who_pays: US taxpayers with unreported foreign accounts, who would face detection and collection of back taxes; foreign financial institutions, which would bear the cost of identifying and reporting US clients; and foreign bond issuers, who would lose the US interest deduction that makes their bonds more attractive to US buyers [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore account holders and foreign banks

drawbacks.text: Foreign financial institutions would bear the cost of building reporting systems and screening every account for US owners, costs that can be passed on to customers through fees [S2] [S3].

The bill's reporting rules apply broadly to institutions and entities abroad, and honest savers with legitimate foreign accounts — for example dual citizens or Americans working overseas — could face added paperwork or the risk of having accounts frozen by institutions that prefer to drop US clients rather than comply [S2] [S3].

Critics of offshore reporting regimes in general argue that compliance costs push financial institutions to simply refuse US customers, and that some capital will move to jurisdictions outside the rules; the bill's own text shows the complexity involved, running to many pages of definitions, thresholds such as an 'at least 80 percent' ownership test, and implementing guidance left to regulators [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is meaningful: closing the offshore reporting gap raises revenue from the wealthiest taxpayers and makes the tax system fairer for everyone who pays honestly. The costs are real but narrower: compliance expenses for foreign banks, more paperwork for Americans with legitimate foreign accounts, and some risk that institutions avoid US clients rather than comply. On balance the bill was designed to shift burdens onto the parties best positioned to detect offshore evasion — the institutions holding the money — rather than onto the IRS or ordinary taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, whose chair was its own sponsor, and it never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles B. Rangel, chair of the House Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on October 27, 2009 [S1].
Eleven House Democrats cosponsored it, but no Republican did [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction and no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — was ever taken [S5].
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US taxpayers with unreported offshore accounts and the foreign institutions serving them avoided the new reporting and withholding regime during this Congress; honest taxpayers did not get the enforcement tool.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore account holders and foreign banks

for.name: Rep. Charles B. Rangel
for.role: Sponsor; chair of the House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee, where it received no further action.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill after it was referred on October 27, 2009.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, so no party split is recorded; the only recorded support was 11 House Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsor [S4].

industries.industry: Foreign financial institutions (banks and brokerages holding US client money)
industries.note: The bill would require them to identify and report US account holders or face consequences, imposing compliance costs; institutions that profit from serving offshore wealth had an interest in the rules never taking effect, which runs against honest taxpayers [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Offshore wealth management and private banking
industries.note: The industry depends on account confidentiality and non-reporting; the bill's reporting requirements would directly shrink its value proposition to US clients seeking to keep income undisclosed [S2] [S3].
The bill denies the tax deduction for interest on non-registered bonds issued outside the United States, making those bonds less attractive and raising their borrowing costs [S2].
